heading: Domain 8 in one view
body: Let us go back over Domain 8, Software Development Security, as you would on the last evening before the exam. It carries 10 percent of the exam. The whole domain has one message. Security is built into software from the first idea until the day that software is retired, and that is true whether you write the software or buy it. When you read a scenario, ask three things. Where in the life cycle are we? What security activity belongs at this point? And does this answer fix the cause, or only a symptom? Most wrong answers in this domain are real controls that are simply in the wrong place, or that arrive too late. Remember that you are an adviser and a manager. You are not the person who writes the patch. Your answers should build security into the process, and leave risk decisions with management.

heading: Life cycle and methods
body: Now the methods. Waterfall runs the stages in strict order, and it suits stable requirements. Spiral repeats loops of goals, risk analysis, prototype and planning, and it suits large, uncertain projects. When you see the words risk-driven or prototype, think spiral. Agile delivers small pieces in short cycles, and Scrum works in sprints of one month or less. The Scaled Agile Framework coordinates many agile teams on one product. DevOps joins development and operations through automation. DevSecOps makes security everyone's shared and automated duty. People often mix up certification and accreditation. Certification is the technical check. Accreditation is management's formal acceptance of the remaining risk. The usual trap is an answer that forces a team back to waterfall. Prefer the answer that builds security into the method the business has already chosen. And prefer finding flaws early, because that is where they cost least.

heading: Maturity models
body: Maturity models are often tested on exact order, so say this aloud. The five CMMI levels, from lowest to highest, are Initial, Managed, Defined, Quantitatively Managed, Optimizing. CMMI stands for Capability Maturity Model Integration. Initial depends on heroes. Managed plans and tracks each project. Defined means one standard process across the organization. Quantitatively Managed means measured and controlled with numbers. Optimizing means continual improvement. Here is what people mix up. In the older model, Level 2 was called Repeatable, and Level 4 was called Managed. So the word Managed moves. The Software Assurance Maturity Model, or SAMM, comes from OWASP, the Open Worldwide Application Security Project. It is about software security specifically. It has five business functions, Governance, Design, Implementation, Verification and Operations, with three practices in each, scored from 1 to 3. Targets should match the organization's risk, so top scores everywhere are not the goal.

heading: Change management and running software
body: Next, life after release. Most of a program's life comes after it goes live, so patching, monitoring and access reviews never stop. When a vendor ends support, plan an upgrade or a replacement, and manage the risk until then. Change management has three parts in a fixed order. Request control, then change control, then release control. Users ask, developers build and test, and then the change is approved for production. Developers should not move their own code into production, because that breaks separation of duties. In an emergency, the paperwork may come afterward, but authorized approval, a way to undo the change and a later review do not go away. So be wary of any answer that lets someone deploy directly because the matter is urgent. Finally, an integrated product team brings together many fields from the start, including legal, purchasing and the business owner. It is wider than DevOps.

heading: The development workshop
body: Now the development ecosystem. Protect the whole workshop and not only the finished product. Memory-safe languages reduce memory flaws, but they do not remove bad logic or injection. Libraries become part of your product, so use approved sources, pin versions and verify hashes. Allow only approved plug-ins in the integrated development environment. Run software with least privilege, and turn off debugging in production. Continuous delivery has a person approve each release, while continuous deployment releases automatically. The pipeline holds the keys to production, so restrict who can change it, keep secrets in a vault, sign what is built and stop the build when security tests fail. Configuration management tells you exactly which versions were shipped. Here is a favorite scenario. A password was committed to a repository and then deleted from the latest version. It remains in the history. The first action is to change the password.

heading: Choosing the right test
body: Testing tools are a classic source of confusion, so let us be exact. Static application security testing, or SAST, reads the source code without running it. It works early, names the exact line and gives more false alarms. Dynamic application security testing, or DAST, attacks the running application from outside. It finds run-time and setup problems, needs no source code and cannot name the line. Interactive application security testing, or IAST, puts an agent inside the application while tests are running. It can name the line, with fewer false alarms, but it sees only the code that the tests reach. Software composition analysis checks third-party components, their known flaws and their licenses. Fuzzing sends unexpected input to cause failures. So look for the clue in the question. If the code cannot run yet, choose static. If you have no source code, choose dynamic. If the concern is borrowed parts, choose composition analysis.

heading: Proving that it works
body: Assessing software security means looking for direct evidence. Change records should show who, what, when, who approved and whether testing passed. Shared accounts break accountability, and logs must be kept where the people being logged cannot alter them. Clocks must be synchronized. Then the key activity is to compare what reached production with what was approved. Statements and policies are weaker evidence than protected records. For the numbers, single loss expectancy equals asset value times exposure factor. Annualized loss expectancy equals single loss expectancy times the annualized rate of occurrence. The value of a fix equals the old yearly loss, minus the new yearly loss, minus the yearly cost of the fix. The most common mistake is forgetting that last subtraction. Severity scores rate the flaw, but your own data and exposure decide the real risk. Senior management accepts residual risk, and ignoring a risk is never acceptable.

heading: Software from someone else
body: Now acquired software. You can outsource the work, but not the accountability for your data. Put security requirements in the contract before signing. With commercial products, you depend on the vendor, so harden the default settings and watch for end of support. Software escrow protects you if the vendor closes down, and a service level agreement does not, because a closed vendor cannot honor it. Open source can be inspected, but that does not prove that anyone did, and its license may carry legal duties. Test what contractors deliver. For managed providers, a Type 2 report shows that controls worked over a period. In the cloud, the provider takes on more as you go from infrastructure, to platform, to software as a service. In every model, you manage your data and your users. A software bill of materials lists the parts in a product, which speeds up your response to a new flaw. It does not prove that the parts are safe.

heading: Memory and injection flaws
body: Let us review two code flaws and their exact fixes. A buffer overflow writes more data than a fixed memory space can hold. The primary fix is checking the length of input against the size of the buffer, along with safe functions or memory-safe languages. Address Space Layout Randomization moves memory locations around. Data Execution Prevention blocks code from running in data areas. Those two make attacks harder, but they do not remove the flaw. SQL injection happens when user input is treated as a database command. SQL is Structured Query Language. The primary fix is a parameterized query, also called a prepared statement, which keeps the command and the data apart. Add server-side validation and least privilege on the database account. Be wary of three tempting answers. Checks only in the browser can be bypassed. A firewall rule treats a symptom. And a stored procedure helps only if it does not join user text into a command.

heading: Scripting, forgery and race conditions
body: These are the flaws people mix up most. In cross-site scripting, an attacker's script runs in the victim's browser through a trusted site. Stored scripting is saved on the server and reaches every visitor. Reflected scripting bounces back from a request, often through a crafted link, and nothing is saved. DOM-based scripting happens in the page's own code. The main fix is output encoding. In cross-site request forgery, a logged-in user's browser is tricked into sending a request that the user never intended. The fix is an anti-forgery token, SameSite cookies and confirmation of sensitive actions. Remember the trust. Scripting abuses the user's trust in the site. Forgery abuses the site's trust in the user's browser. A race condition, such as time of check to time of use, is a gap between checking something and using it. The fix is an atomic action, a lock or a database transaction. Input validation does not help.

heading: APIs, standards and choosing the best answer
body: Finally, application programming interfaces, or APIs. Check every request for the specific object being requested, because being logged in does not give the right to see another person's record. OAuth 2.0 is delegated authorization, and OpenID Connect adds authentication. Rate limiting slows abuse, but it does not fix a missing authorization check. Secure coding standards work only with management support, training and automated checks. Fail securely, keep error details in protected logs and never invent your own cryptography. Software-defined security manages rules centrally so that they follow workloads, which makes the central console a prime target. Now, how to choose. Look for the answer that fixes the cause, in the code or in the process. Prefer early over late, and automatic over manual. Prefer evidence over promises. Let management accept the risk, and put people's safety first. Trust your preparation, read each question carefully, and take your time.
